title: Episode 305: Henry IV: The Usurpation of 1399, the House of Lancaster, and the Battle of Shrewsbury
description:
The turbulent thirteen-year reign of King Henry IV, the first Lancastrian king of England. Usurping the throne from his cousin Richard II in 1399, Henry found that seizing the crown was far easier than wearing it. Beset by financial insolvency, parliamentary strife, religious unrest, and persistent assassination plots, Henry faced a massive Welsh national uprising led by Owain Glyndŵr and a treasonous rebellion by his former northern allies, the mighty Percy family. At the blood-drenched Battle of Shrewsbury in 1403, Henry fought hand-to-hand in the royal vanguard to defeat Harry Hotspur. Plagued by debilitating illness and haunted by guilt, discover the sovereign whose agonizing reign gave birth to Shakespeare's immortal phrase: 'Uneasy lies the head that wears a crown.'

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, our Kings and Queens of England series examines the founder of the House of Lancaster: the formidable warrior-nobleman who deposed a tyrant only to spend every day of his reign fighting for his survival: King Henry IV. Here is George with the dramatic story of Bolingbroke, Owain Glyndŵr, and Harry Hotspur.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE HEIR OF GAUNT: FROM BOLINGBROKE TO EXILED CHAMPION: 1367 TO 1399
Born in April 1367 at Bolingbroke Castle in Lincolnshire, Henry was the eldest son of John of Gaunt, Duke of Lancaster, and Blanche of Lancaster. From his birth, Henry was destined for martial prominence, endowed with athletic strength, sharp intelligence, and a devout religious temperament. As a young knight, he gained renown across Europe: he fought alongside the Teutonic Knights during crusades in Prussia and Lithuania, traveled as a pilgrim to the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem, and defeated France's champion knights at the grand jousts of Saint-Inglevert. As Earl of Derby, he joined the Lords Appellant in 1387 to curb the abuses of his cousin Richard II, demonstrating tactical brilliance at Radcot Bridge. Yet Henry remained fundamentally moderate, seeking to reconcile with Richard. But Richard never forgot. In 1398, when Henry quarreled with Thomas Mowbray, Richard banished Henry into foreign exile for ten years. When John of Gaunt died in 1399, Richard revoked the inheritance, confiscating the vast Lancastrian estates that spanned across thirty counties. Henry was left landless, disinherited, and destitute in Paris. Surrounded by fellow exiles, he realized that his only choice was total submission or armed revolution. He chose revolution. Bolingbroke's travels in eastern Europe were legendary: he had commanded three hundred English knights and archers on crusade in Lithuania, besieged Vilnius, and made a personal pilgrimage to Venice and the Holy Land, earning a continental reputation as one of the most accomplished and pious knights of his generation. His deep learning, fluent French and Latin, and mastery of theology made him an intellectual heavyweight among the English aristocracy.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE LANCASTRIAN COUP: CLAIMING THE CROWN AT WESTMINSTER
In July 1399, taking advantage of Richard's absence in Ireland, Henry landed at Ravenspur on the Yorkshire coast with just three ships and sixty loyal men. He swore a solemn oath on the relics of Bridlington Priory that he came only to recover his father's rightful inheritance, not to usurp the crown. Great northern lords, including Henry Percy, Earl of Northumberland, and Ralph Neville, Earl of Westmorland, rushed to his standard with thousands of armed retainers. As Henry marched south, support for the despotic Richard evaporated like morning mist. When Richard surrendered at Flint Castle, Henry found himself master of the entire realm. But inheriting the crown posed a profound constitutional dilemma: if lineage alone dictated succession, the rightful heir was eight-year-old Edmund Mortimer, Earl of March, descended from Lionel of Antwerp, the second son of Edward III, whereas Henry was the son of John of Gaunt, the third son. Henry deftly bypassed this obstacle by appealing to popular acclaim, conquest, and the incompetence of Richard. On September 30, 1399, in Westminster Hall, Henry rose from his seat, crossed himself on the forehead and breast, and in clear English proclaimed his right to the realm. Crowned on the Feast of St. Edward the Confessor, Henry anointed himself with sacred holy oil supposedly given by the Virgin Mary to St. Thomas Becket, establishing the Lancastrian dynasty. When Henry stood before Parliament to claim the crown, he delivered his historic address not in the Anglo-Norman French of the court, but in the native English tongue: 'In the name of Fader, Son, and Holy Gost, I, Henry of Lancaster, chalenge this Rewme of Yngland.' By delivering his claim in the vernacular, Henry deliberately bound his new dynasty to the common national identity of the English people.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: UNEASY LIES THE HEAD: THE EPIPHANY RISING AND RELIGIOUS PERSECUTION
Henry quickly discovered the bitter truth of royal power: seizing a throne by force invited others to do the same. In January 1400, barely three months after his glittering coronation, a conspiracy of Richard's loyalist nobles, the Epiphany Rising, plotted to assassinate Henry and his sons during a Twelfth Night tournament at Windsor Castle. Warned at the eleventh hour by the Earl of Rutland, Henry fled through the winter night to London, rallied the citizens, and crushed the conspirators, whose severed heads were delivered in sacks to Newgate. Shortly thereafter, the imprisoned Richard II died mysteriously at Pontefract Castle, ensuring no focal point for royalist rebellion remained alive. To cement his alliance with the powerful Catholic Church and court conservative clerical support, Henry enacted the notorious statute De Heretico Comburendo in 1401—the first law in English history authorizing the burning of heretics at the stake. Targeting the growing Lollard movement, followers of John Wycliffe who preached against church corruption and transubstantiation, the statute unleashed terrifying inquisitorial fires across England, claiming martyrs like the tailor John Badby, who was burned in an empty barrel at Smithfield despite the young Prince of Wales pleading with him to recant. The burning of John Badby at Smithfield illustrated the chilling cruelty of the anti-Lollard crusade: when Badby screamed in agony inside the blazing barrel, Prince Hal ordered the fire quenched and offered the condemned tailor a royal pension if he would recant his heresy. Badby steadfastly refused, and the prince ordered the barrel rekindled, burning him to ash, a stark warning to all religious dissenters.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: OWAIN GLYNDŴR AND THE WELSH WAR OF INDEPENDENCE: 1400 TO 1405
While Henry battled plots in England, a catastrophic storm broke across the western border. In September 1400, Owain Glyndŵr, a charismatic Welsh nobleman and descendant of ancient Welsh princes, was proclaimed Prince of Wales by his countrymen, raising the dragon banner in a war of national independence. Burning English border towns like Ruthin and Oswestry to the ground, Glyndŵr unleashed guerrilla warfare across the craggy mountains of Snowdonia and the valleys of Powys. Henry led three massive punitive expeditions into Wales, but each campaign was thwarted by relentless, torrential rainstorms, freezing blizzards, and washed-out roads—weather so astonishingly brutal that English soldiers whispered Glyndŵr was a wizard who commanded the demonic spirits of the air. In 1402, Glyndŵr routed an English army at the Battle of Bryn Glas, capturing Sir Edmund Mortimer, uncle to the young claimant to the English throne. When Henry refused to pay Mortimer's ransom, Mortimer defected, marrying Glyndŵr's daughter. Glyndŵr then concluded the Tripartite Indenture with the Percys and Mortimers, boldly planning to carve England and Wales into three sovereign realms. Owain captured the mighty coastal fortresses of Harlech and Aberystwyth, holding sovereign parliaments and securing military aid from the King of France. Glyndŵr's guerrilla campaign was masterminded with exceptional psychological acumen: his Welsh archers fired from hidden wooded ridges, vanishing into the mist before royal cavalry could deploy. His capture of Harlech Castle gave him a formidable coastal citadel from which he could receive French naval supplies, while his vision for Wales included an independent Welsh church and two national universities.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE PERCY REBELLION AND HARRY HOTSPUR: 1403
The deadliest threat to Henry's survival came not from his foreign enemies, but from the very men who had placed the crown upon his head: the Percys of Northumberland. The Earl of Northumberland and his impetuous, legendary warrior son, Sir Henry Percy—universally known as Harry Hotspur for the ferocity of his cavalry charges—believed King Henry had treated them with unpardonable ingratitude. The Crown owed the Percys astronomical sums for garrisoning the Scottish border and fighting the Scots at Homildon Hill, where Hotspur had captured the Earl of Douglas. When King Henry forbade Hotspur from ransoming his Scottish prisoners and refused to redeem his brother-in-law Mortimer from Welsh captivity, Hotspur's fiery temper exploded into open treason. In July 1403, Hotspur rode south from the Scottish Marches with a veteran army of seasoned northern knights, uniting with his uncle Thomas Percy, Earl of Worcester, and Cheshire archers who still wore the white hart badge of Richard II. Issuing a public manifesto denouncing Henry as a perjured usurper who had broken his solemn oath at Ravenspur, Hotspur marched toward Shrewsbury, intending to join forces with Owain Glyndŵr and seize the western midlands. Henry realized that if Hotspur and Glyndŵr united, the Lancastrian cause was doomed. The feud between Henry and the Percys was ignited by money and pride: the king had showered land on other favorites while leaving the Percys to personally finance the defenses of the Scottish border. Hotspur's wife was Elizabeth Mortimer, making him fiercely devoted to the Mortimer claim; when Henry accused Hotspur of being a traitor to his face in council, Hotspur reportedly placed his hand on his sword, shouting that he would shed his blood before submitting to tyranny.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE BLOODY CLASH AT SHREWSBURY: JULY 21, 1403
Marching at breakneck speed, King Henry reached Shrewsbury mere hours before Hotspur could seize the walled town, cutting him off from the Welsh border. On July 21, 1403, the two armies drew up their lines outside the town in fields of dense, ripe peas. The Battle of Shrewsbury was the first major clash in history where English longbowmen fought against English longbowmen on both sides. When the trumpet sounded, the sky turned black as hundreds of thousands of arrows crossed in midair. Cheshire archers on Hotspur's side unleashed a devastating initial volley that cut down royal troops in rows; royal vanguard commander the Earl of Stafford was slain instantly. Sixteen-year-old Prince Hal, fighting in the royal center, was struck in the face by an arrow that penetrated six inches beneath his right eye into his jawbone. Refusing to leave the field, the bloody young prince insisted on fighting on to inspire his men. Hotspur and Douglas led an all-or-nothing desperate cavalry charge straight toward the royal standard, cutting down several knights dressed in the king's royal coat of armor as decoys. But suddenly, as Hotspur raised his visor to breathe in the suffocating heat, an anonymous arrow pierced his throat. As Hotspur crashed to the earth, the cry echoed across the field: 'Harry Percy is dead!' The rebel line shattered into panicked flight, and King Henry emerged victorious from the bloodiest field of his life. Prince Hal's survival at Shrewsbury was an extraordinary testament to medieval surgery: the arrow had sheared off its wooden shaft, leaving the barbed iron point wedged in the bone of his skull. Surgeon Bradmore used hollow elderberry wood and rose honey as antiseptics to keep the prince alive during the agonizing extraction, a wound that left Hal with a deep scar on his cheek for the rest of his life.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE BROKEN MONARCH AND THE JERUSALEM CHAMBER: 1406 TO 1413
Though victorious at Shrewsbury and finally breaking the Percy power at Bramham Moor in 1408, Henry paid a devastating price. In 1405, following another northern conspiracy, Henry made the fateful decision to execute Richard le Scrope, the Archbishop of York—the first judicial execution of a prelate in English history. According to contemporary chroniclers, the exact moment the executioner's sword struck the archbishop's neck, King Henry was struck by a sudden, agonizing seizure. For the remainder of his life, Henry was tormented by a horrific, disfiguring skin disease—widely believed to be leprosy or advanced cardiovascular decay—along with crippling epileptic fits that left him semi-paralyzed. Popular belief held that God had cursed him for murdering an anointed archbishop. In his final years, Henry watched his energetic son Prince Hal clash with him for control of the Royal Council. Henry had long believed a prophecy that he would die in Jerusalem after embarking on a glorious crusade. On March 20, 1413, while praying at Westminster Abbey, the forty-five-year-old king suffered a final, catastrophic stroke. Carried into the Abbot's lodgings, he opened his eyes, asked where he was, and was told the room was called the Jerusalem Chamber. Henry murmured that the prophecy was fulfilled, breathed his last, and passed the crown to his warrior son, Henry V. Henry's debilitating illness caused his flesh to rot while he was still alive, leading superstitious courtiers to murmur that the Holy Oil he had used at his coronation had turned to poison. As Prince Hal pushed his father to abdicate in favor of the younger generation, father and son clashed in agonizing emotional scenes, with Henry weeping in the Jerusalem Chamber as he questioned whether his dynasty would survive.

[Rebecca - Host]
